strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: improving generalization of protein ML models to individual proteins under data scarcity and distribution shift.
Broad empirical evaluation across three protein tasks (fitness, structure, function) and multiple models/scales, including standard benchmarks such as ProteinGym and CAMEO.
Method is simple and clearly described, building on the prevalent Y-shaped masked-language-modeling paradigm, making it easy to implement in existing protein models.
Uses LoRA and gradient accumulation to make test-time training feasible on a single GPU for large models, with hyperparameters and validation protocols documented.
Constructs a new MaveDB-based validation set for fitness prediction to avoid test-set leakage and support hyperparameter tuning.
Reports improvements on challenging structure targets and establishes a marginal new state-of-the-art on ProteinGym.
Reproducibility statement and appendix provide substantial experimental details, including model adaptations and dataset construction.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: test-time training (TTT) is well established in computer vision and NLP; applying it to proteins via existing masked-language-modeling objectives is a straightforward adaptation rather than a new algorithmic contribution.

Empirical gains are often marginal: SaProt (650M) + TTT improves ProteinGym Avg. Spearman only from 0.4569 to 0.4583, and ESM2 (650M) + TTT from 0.4139 to 0.4153. Function prediction gains are below 1% absolute on mAP/AUROC/accuracy/MCC/F1.

The 'new state-of-the-art' claim on ProteinGym is overstated: the improvement over TranceptEVE L is 0.0024 and over SaProt is 0.0014, with standard deviations around 0.00001; the reported '40% higher improvement' framing is unclear and not practically convincing.

Structure prediction evaluation uses only 18 filtered 'challenging' CAMEO targets, which may overrepresent cases where TTT helps; broader generalization and failure modes are not systematically analyzed.

Function prediction comparisons are weak: only the base models are used as baselines, without comparison to other modern protein function prediction methods; the tasks (TPS substrate classification and subcellular localization) are niche and improvements may be within practical noise.

The theoretical link to perplexity minimization is nearly tautological: TTT directly minimizes the masked language modeling loss, which is perplexity; correlational evidence between perplexity and downstream performance does not establish that perplexity reduction is the mechanism behind TTT gains.
The paper does not thoroughly investigate when TTT helps or hurts. It acknowledges some degraded predictions but offers no systematic failure-mode analysis or mitigation strategies.
Computational overhead is not fully characterized for large-scale benchmarks such as ProteinGym, where TTT must be run per protein across 217 proteins and millions of mutations.

The zero-shot fitness evaluation uses TTT on the test protein sequence, which is a transductive adaptation; while valid in a test-time adaptation setting, it is not directly comparable to strict zero-shot methods and the positioning could be clearer.
Methodological depth is limited: no exploration of alternative self-supervised objectives, masking strategies, regularization, or architectural choices beyond default pre-training settings.
Reproducibility is only promised: code and the new dataset splits are not yet available, and exact reproduction of the filtered benchmarks may require nontrivial effort.
Potential dual-use or ethical implications of improved protein fitness/structure/function prediction are not discussed, albeit this is a minor concern relative to the technical weaknesses.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical problem: per-protein adaptation when labeled data are scarce and distribution shifts matter.
The proposed TTT is simple, broadly applicable to Y-shaped protein models, and can be plugged into existing masked-language-model backbones.
The authors evaluate across three different downstream tasks (fitness, structure, function) and multiple models/scales, which provides useful initial evidence.
The manuscript is generally clear, with detailed experimental appendices and a reproducibility statement promising code release.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: test-time training via self-supervised masked modeling is well established in vision/NLP, and the adaptation to protein single sequences is an application rather than a new method.

The theoretical link to perplexity minimization is essentially tautological: minimizing the masked LM loss on a single sequence minimizes its perplexity by definition; no new formal result or deeper insight is provided.

Empirical gains are marginal and often within noise or practically negligible: e.g., SaProt 650M + TTT improves ProteinGym Avg. Spearman from 0.4569 to 0.4583, with some phenotype categories decreasing; function gains are ~0.006-0.009.

The claim of new state-of-the-art on ProteinGym is overstated: the improvement over SaProt 650M is tiny and not clearly separated from baseline/benchmark variance; no proper significance testing across proteins is reported.

Evaluation is selective and potentially optimistic: structure results are only on 18 challenging CAMEO targets filtered by pLDDT<70 and perplexity>=6, and TTT step selection uses pLDDT on the test protein.

Baselines and comparisons are insufficient: for structure, ESM3+CoT is not matched in step/selection budget; for fitness and function, simple adaptation baselines (e.g., MSA-based fine-tuning, ESM variant scoring, calibration) are missing or not fully compared.

The transductive nature of TTT is not adequately discussed: the model is fine-tuned on the exact test protein sequence, and for fitness this can change the log-odds calibration; possible leakage/overfitting to the wild-type sequence is not analyzed.

Hyperparameter selection undermines the 'on the fly' claim: optimal TTT steps are tuned on separate validation sets or via pLDDT, which is unavailable for many single-protein use cases; failure modes and robustness are largely deferred to future work.
The paper does not provide a rigorous analysis of when TTT helps or hurts; Figure 9 shows degradations for some proteins, but no systematic study of failure modes or conditions.
Reproducibility is partially promised but not yet demonstrated; details are in appendix, but code/data release and exact leaderboard comparison methodology remain unclear.

strengths: Introduces a broadly applicable test-time training (TTT) approach for proteins that adapts self-supervised protein language models to individual test proteins without labels or additional target-specific data.
Evaluates TTT across three important protein tasks—fitness, structure, and function—and across multiple models and model scales, demonstrating practical breadth.
Structure prediction results are the strongest: TTT substantially improves ESMFold and ESM3 on challenging CAMEO targets and outperforms masked-prediction and chain-of-thought baselines.
Provides a plausible and empirically supported link between masked-language-modeling TTT and perplexity reduction, including correlation analyses between perplexity and structure quality.
The paper includes extensive experimental details, hyperparameter grids, dataset construction protocols, and a reproducibility statement promising code release.
weaknesses: The protein fitness and function prediction gains are very small in absolute terms (e.g., SaProt on ProteinGym improves from 0.4569 to 0.4583; TPS mAP from 0.805 to 0.811), making the state-of-the-art and '40% higher improvement' claims overstated without statistical significance or practical-significance analysis.

The structure evaluation is limited to 18 challenging CAMEO targets preselected using low pLDDT and high perplexity, which may bias results toward cases where TTT is likely to help; broader performance across less challenging targets is not established.

The perplexity-minimization explanation is informal rather than rigorous: the MLM loss is only directly equal to log-perplexity in special cases, and the argument does not provide a formal guarantee that lower perplexity implies better downstream performance.

For fitness and function prediction, optimal hyperparameters and TTT step counts are selected using validation datasets, which weakens the claim that TTT requires no additional data and may not be feasible for truly novel individual proteins without representative validation data.

Computational cost and scalability are not fully characterized across all models and tasks; per-protein fine-tuning may be expensive at proteome scale, and inference-time overhead is reported mainly for ESM3.
TTT is not uniformly beneficial—some models/datasets show no improvement or small degradation—and failure modes are acknowledged but not systematically analyzed.
Function prediction baselines are relatively weak or restricted (PLM-only TerpeneMiner, older Light attention), so it is unclear how much TTT would help against stronger current baselines.

strengths: Introduces a simple, general, and easy-to-implement test-time customization method for protein language models, with a user-friendly open-source implementation.
Broad empirical validation across three major protein tasks (structure, fitness, function) and multiple model families and scales, showing mostly consistent improvements.
Strong case studies on challenging problems: antibody-antigen loop modeling and viral protein structure expansion in BFVD, where general-purpose models struggle.
Careful mitigation of data leakage, e.g., using ESMFold v0 for CAMEO, constructing a disjoint MaveDB validation set, and avoiding ProteinGym overlap.
Efficient implementation using LoRA, SGD, and gradient accumulation, enabling customization of billion-parameter models on a single GPU with acceptable runtime.
Provides insights linking customization to perplexity minimization, and shows robustness of pLDDT-based step selection for structure prediction.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core idea is an application of existing test-time training / masked language modeling adaptation to protein LMs, rather than a new learning algorithm.

Performance gains are often very small, especially for fitness and function prediction (e.g., ProSST on ProteinGym improves by ~0.002 Spearman; some phenotype-specific results even regress). Claims of 'new state-of-the-art' are therefore overstated.

For structure prediction, the evaluation set is small (18 CAMEO test targets) and selected based on low ESMFold confidence, which may not reflect general performance; statistical significance over targets is not reported.

The method relies on a confidence function (e.g., pLDDT) to select the best customization step in structure prediction. When such a confidence signal is unavailable or unreliable, hyperparameter selection becomes more difficult and the claimed 'on-the-fly' robustness is weakened.

The paper claims 'without assuming any additional data,' but hyperparameters are tuned on validation sets and pLDDT selection uses the pretrained downstream head. The distinction between target-specific data and global tuning data should be clearer.

Baselines are somewhat limited: no comparison to alternative test-time adaptation methods, full fine-tuning, or simple ensembling beyond ESMFold + MP / ESM3 + CoT; no comparison to MSA-based structure predictors on the same challenging CAMEO targets.
The theoretical justification linking perplexity minimization to downstream performance is mostly correlational and does not provide formal guarantees or a rigorous causal explanation.

The title and several claims ('One protein is all you need', 'first customization method in machine learning for biology') are overclaims that do not accurately reflect the dependence on large-scale pretraining and the incremental nature of the contribution.

strengths: Introduces a simple and general test-time customization method for protein language models via masked language modeling, applicable to multiple backbones and downstream tasks.
Provides a user-friendly implementation and a detailed experimental appendix, supporting reproducibility.
Evaluates on several tasks (structure, fitness, function) and models (ESMFold, ESM3, HelixFold, ESM2, SaProt, ProSST, MSA Transformer), which gives a broad empirical picture.
Includes two practical case studies (antibody-antigen loops and viral protein structures in BFVD) that illustrate potential biological utility on challenging examples.
Uses LoRA and gradient accumulation to make customization feasible for large protein models, and reports runtime analysis showing acceptable overhead relative to AlphaFold2.
Extends the approach to multiple sequence alignments and validates fitness performance on an independently constructed MaveDB dataset.
Addresses an important practical problem: improving predictions for individual proteins when additional labeled data are unavailable.
weaknesses: The core method is largely an application of existing test-time training / masked autoencoder ideas to protein language models; algorithmic novelty is limited for a top-tier AI venue.

Reported gains are often marginal, e.g., ProteinGym ProSST improves from 0.5068 to 0.5087 and TPS mAP from 0.805 to 0.811, which does not strongly support claims of new state-of-the-art or consistent substantial improvement.

There is a fairness concern: ProteinTTT performs unsupervised fine-tuning on the test protein, which differs from the standard zero-shot ProteinGym setting; comparisons to zero-shot baselines are therefore not apples-to-apples.

No comparison is made to other test-time adaptation methods or to a control fine-tuning baseline (e.g., fine-tuning on a random or unrelated protein), so it is unclear whether gains come from target-specific customization or from generic additional fine-tuning.
Structure prediction is evaluated on only 18 low-confidence CAMEO targets, a biased subset; full-benchmark results and formal statistical significance tests are missing.

For structure prediction, the final custom step is selected using pLDDT from the downstream head, which is a form of test-time model selection and may not transfer to tasks without reliable confidence measures.

The BFVD case study validates largely against AlphaFold2 predictions rather than experimental structures; cross-method pLDDT comparability is not established, making the claimed 19% improvement weak and potentially circular.
The antibody-antigen case study compares only to ESMFold, not to AlphaFold2 or antibody-specific methods, so its practical significance over strong baselines is unclear.

The theoretical justification linking perplexity minimization to downstream improvement is informal and correlational; reducing single-sequence perplexity could also reflect overfitting rather than improved representation.
Hyperparameter sensitivity and overfitting are acknowledged; fixed-step customization for fitness and function may be suboptimal and lacks a per-protein confidence-based stopping criterion.
Function prediction is only a small proof-of-concept with tiny gains and limited analysis.
There is no systematic failure-mode analysis, despite per-protein results showing that customization sometimes degrades predictions.

The title and abstract overclaim relative to the evidence: phrases such as 'One Protein Is All You Need', 'first customization method', and 'expanding known structures' are stronger than what is demonstrated.

strengths: Introduces ProteinTTT, a simple and general method for self-supervised test-time customization of masked protein language models to individual target proteins without requiring additional data; it is applicable to multiple Y-shaped architectures and downstream heads.

Provides broad empirical validation across protein structure, fitness, and function prediction, multiple models and model scales, and two challenging case studies, showing consistent improvements especially on out-of-distribution targets.
Strong reproducibility: user-friendly implementation, code snippets, detailed hyperparameters, datasets, and experimental setups are provided.
Offers useful insight by linking test-time customization to perplexity minimization and demonstrating correlation between perplexity reduction and downstream prediction quality.
The antibody-antigen loop and viral protein case studies demonstrate practical biological utility and potential impact in computational biology.
weaknesses: The core method is a fairly direct adaptation of existing test-time training and masked language model fine-tuning to proteins, so algorithmic novelty is limited; the claim of being the first customization method in machine learning for biology may be overbroad.

Several reported improvements are very small, e.g., ProSST fitness improves from 0.5068 to 0.5087 and function prediction gains are under one point, with some phenotype metrics decreasing; practical significance and robustness beyond seed variance are not fully established.

Structure prediction evaluation on CAMEO uses only 18 low-confidence test targets and improvements over the masked prediction baseline are modest; selecting steps via pLDDT may bias toward confidence rather than true accuracy, although correlation with LDDT is shown.

The BFVD case study largely defines improvement through pLDDT and validates against AlphaFold2 high-confidence structures, which may themselves be unreliable for out-of-distribution viral proteins; broader experimental validation is limited.

No direct comparison to other test-time adaptation or customization methods beyond simple baselines such as masked prediction and chain-of-thought; fitness and function evaluations mainly compare against base models only.
Hyperparameter sensitivity and the lack of per-target validation when no confidence function exists may limit applicability, and the method can overfit to a single target sequence.
Claims such as state-of-the-art performance and expanding known structures are somewhat stronger than what the marginal average gains and pLDDT-based validation fully support.
